title: Stock Detail chart panes: allow enlarging to full screen or dragging taller
description:
User-requested feature: on the Stock Detail page, the chart panes should be able to enlarge -- either to full screen, or by dragging to increase their height -- instead of being stuck at their current fixed size. Confirmed via reading the current code before writing this task: `StockCharts.tsx` composes four separate Lightweight Charts instances stacked vertically -- `PriceChart` (candlestick + overlays, `CHART_HEIGHT = 320`), `OscillatorChart`, `VolumeIndicatorsChart`, and `TrendStrengthChart` (each `CHART_HEIGHT = 420`) -- each with its own hardcoded pixel height and no existing resize/fullscreen affordance of any kind (grepped for `fullscreen`/`resize`/`ResizeObserver` across all four files -- none found).

Important existing constraint that simplifies this: every chart is created via the shared `frontend/src/utils/chart.ts`'s `createBaseChart(container)`, which already passes `autoSize: true` to Lightweight Charts -- the library already installs its own internal `ResizeObserver` on the container and redraws the chart to fill whatever size that container actually is. This means implementing this feature is primarily a container/layout + UI-affordance problem (give the container a way to become bigger), NOT a problem of manually calling the chart's own resize API -- `chart.resize()`/`applyOptions({width, height})` calls should not be needed for the normal case, since the library already reacts to its container's size changing out from under it.

The user's phrasing ("enlarge to full screen OR drag bigger in height") leaves two real UX approaches on the table rather than picking one -- research and decide (record as a `decisions` entry, don't just pick one silently):
- A full-screen toggle (an expand icon/button on each chart, or one for the whole `StockCharts` stack) that makes the chart occupy the full viewport, then a visible way to exit back to the normal layout. Decide between the browser's native Fullscreen API (`element.requestFullscreen()` -- real OS-level fullscreen, but has permission-prompt/browser-support quirks and needs an explicit user gesture) versus a CSS-only "maximize within the page" overlay (a fixed-position, viewport-filling `Box` with a high z-index and a close affordance -- simpler, no browser permission dance, but not literally OS fullscreen).
- A drag handle at the bottom edge of a chart's container that lets the user manually resize its height (a `cursor: ns-resize` handle + pointer-event drag tracking, with sane min/max height bounds so a chart can't be dragged to something unusably small or absurdly tall).
- Or both, as separate independent affordances a user can pick between.

Also decide (and record) scope: the user said "graphs" (plural) and "detail view", and all four chart panes share the exact same underlying pattern (own `CHART_HEIGHT` constant, own `createBaseChart`-created instance) -- so the default assumption should be that whatever mechanism is built applies uniformly to all four panes via a shared affordance (a common wrapper component or hook under `components/common/` per Frontend.md §3's placement rule, since this is generic "a container that can enlarge" behavior, not something specific to candlesticks vs. oscillators), not just `PriceChart` alone -- but confirm this reads correctly against the four components' actual structure before committing to a specific implementation shape, since `PriceChart` also owns its own range/interval selector UI above the chart canvas that a naive fullscreen wrapper might need to carry along (or deliberately leave behind, if the fullscreen view is meant to show just the chart).

checklist.step: Research and decide the interaction model: full-screen toggle, drag-to-resize height handle, or both. For a full-screen toggle, decide between the native Fullscreen API and a CSS-only full-viewport overlay. For drag-to-resize, decide min/max height bounds and whether the resized height persists (e.g. localStorage) across reloads/navigation or resets every mount. Record as a `decisions` entry with rationale.

Decide and record the component-placement/reuse shape: a shared `components/common/` wrapper or hook that each of the four chart panes (`PriceChart`, `OscillatorChart`, `VolumeIndicatorsChart`, `TrendStrengthChart`) opts into, versus a per-component implementation -- given all four already share `createBaseChart`'s `autoSize: true` behavior and the same fixed-`CHART_HEIGHT` pattern, prefer a shared mechanism unless something concrete about `PriceChart`'s extra range/interval selector UI genuinely rules that out.

Implement the chosen affordance(s) on all four chart panes (or record a narrower, deliberate scope decision if genuinely warranted), relying on Lightweight Charts' existing `autoSize: true` to handle the actual chart redraw once the container's size changes -- verify this assumption holds in practice (the chart should resize itself without any manual `chart.resize()` call) rather than just assuming it from the option name.

Handle narrow/mobile viewports sensibly for whichever affordance is chosen (e.g. a drag handle needs a reasonable touch-friendly hit target; a full-screen overlay needs to actually fit a small viewport without its own scroll/layout breaking).

Tests (vitest/Testing Library, no live network calls): the toggle/drag interaction itself (simulated pointer events for drag-resize, simulated click + state check for a fullscreen toggle), the min/max height clamping if drag-resize is implemented, and Storybook coverage for any new piece that lands in `components/common/` per Frontend.md §3's placement rule.

decisions.decision: Implement BOTH a full-screen toggle AND an independent drag-to-resize height handle on every chart pane, rather than picking just one. The full-screen toggle is a CSS-only "maximize within the page" overlay, not the native browser Fullscreen API. Drag-resize is clamped to [200px, 900px] (`CHART_FRAME_MIN_HEIGHT`/`CHART_FRAME_MAX_HEIGHT` in `components/common/ChartFrame/ChartFrame.tsx`) and is plain `useState` -- NOT persisted to `localStorage` -- so it resets on an actual remount (page reload, or navigating away and back if the route unmounts the chart) but survives a ticker change within the same mounted chart component.
decisions.rationale: The user's own phrasing ('enlarge to full screen OR drag bigger in height') left both affordances on the table rather than picking one, and the two solve genuinely different problems (full screen for a deep, distraction-free look; drag-resize for a quick 'give me 100 more pixels' without leaving the rest of the page) -- implementing both cost little extra given the shared `ChartFrame` wrapper (decided separately below) does most of the work once. Native `element.requestFullscreen()` was considered and rejected for the full-screen toggle: it needs a direct user-gesture call stack (awkward once routed through a `Tooltip`/`IconButton` click handler), its exact behavior/permission UX varies across browsers and embedded webviews, and it wouldn't have been testable at all in this app's jsdom-based vitest suite -- a CSS-only overlay (`position: fixed; inset: 0`) gets the same practical 'see this chart much bigger' outcome with none of that, at the cost of not being literal OS-level fullscreen. 200px/900px bounds: 200px is short enough to meaningfully shrink a pane but still tall enough to read candles/lines on; 900px is comfortably larger than every existing `CHART_HEIGHT` (320/420) without being so tall a single pane could exceed most monitors' usable height before a drag even reaches the point of needing full screen instead. No `localStorage` persistence: a dragged height is treated as a transient viewing preference for the current page visit, not a durable per-chart setting worth the added complexity of a storage key per pane (4 panes, potentially per-ticker) and a migration story if the key shape ever changed -- this can be revisited as a follow-up if real usage shows people want it to stick across reloads.

decisions.decision: Built a single shared `components/common/ChartFrame/ChartFrame.tsx` wrapper (a render-prop component, not a bare hook) that all four chart panes (`PriceChart`, `OscillatorChart`, `VolumeIndicatorsChart`, `TrendStrengthChart`) wrap their existing returned JSX in, rather than a per-component implementation or a narrower scope (e.g. `PriceChart` only).
decisions.rationale: `ChartFrame` is domain-agnostic (Frontend.md Sec 3's common/-vs-feature-specific placement test): it takes a `label` string and a `defaultHeight` number, with zero reference to tickers/indicators/signals, and every one of the four panes needs the identical maximize/drag-resize mechanics on top of the identical `createBaseChart`/`autoSize: true`/fixed-`CHART_HEIGHT` pattern they already shared -- a textbook case for a shared `common/` component rather than four copies of the same state machine. A render-prop (`children: (args) => ReactNode`) was chosen over wrapping a fixed children subtree because each pane needs two different things threaded into two different places in its own markup: the current `canvasHeight` into its own chart-container `Box`'s `sx.height` (replacing its own `CHART_HEIGHT` constant), and the `maximizeToggle` button placed inline within its own existing controls row (`PriceChart`'s range/interval `ToggleButtonGroup` row; the other three panes' plain title row). `PriceChart`'s extra range/interval selector UI, flagged in the task description as a possible reason to scope this narrower, turned out not to rule out the shared wrapper at all -- the full-screen view just carries that selector UI along inside the maximized pane (it's rendered by the same `children` call either way), which reads naturally: a user maximizing the price chart almost certainly still wants to change the range/interval while looking at it.

decisions.decision: The full-screen overlay is a single `Box` that is ALWAYS rendered at the same position in `ChartFrame`'s own React tree (never conditionally swapped for a `Dialog`/`Modal`), with only its `sx`/ARIA props toggling between in-flow and `{ position: 'fixed', inset: 0, ... }` maximized styling. An initial implementation used MUI's `Dialog` (`fullScreen` + portaled, mount-on-`open`) instead, and had to be reverted after discovering a real bug.
decisions.rationale: `PriceChart`/`OscillatorChart`/`VolumeIndicatorsChart`/`TrendStrengthChart` each create their Lightweight Charts instance in a `useEffect` keyed only on their own query data (`historyQuery.data`/`indicatorsQuery.data`), on the implicit assumption that their own `containerRef` div stays mounted for the chart's whole lifetime -- none of those effects depend on this task's new maximize state. Wrapping the pane's content in a conditionally-rendered `Dialog` changes that content's ancestor chain (nothing, vs. `Dialog > DialogContent`) between the non-maximized and maximized renders; React treats that as the child subtree moving to a different position in the tree, so it unmounts the OLD subtree (destroying the DOM node `containerRef` pointed at, including the chart's own canvas) and mounts a brand NEW one -- but the chart-creation effect's own dependencies hadn't changed, so it never re-ran, leaving the freshly-mounted maximized container with no chart in it at all. This was caught by a real-browser Playwright walkthrough against the actual running dev server (ad hoc, not committed) per this task's explicit instruction to verify the `autoSize` assumption in practice rather than trust it from the option's name -- the mocked `lightweight-charts` unit tests never exercise a real container element, so they never would have caught it. Switching to one persistent `Box` whose own `sx` toggles between normal in-flow layout and a fixed full-viewport overlay keeps the chart's container div mounted the entire time; only its ANCESTOR's CSS position changes, which is exactly the kind of container-size change Lightweight Charts' `autoSize`/internal `ResizeObserver` already handles correctly (confirmed in the same real-browser walkthrough: the `<canvas>` element Lightweight Charts draws onto grew along with the resized/maximized container in every one of the four panes, with zero manual `chart.resize()` calls anywhere in this app's code). The tradeoff: losing `Dialog`'s free scroll-lock/Escape-handling/focus-placement, reimplemented directly in `ChartFrame`'s own `useEffect` (body `overflow: hidden` while maximized, a `keydown` listener for Escape, initial focus on the overlay) instead.

decisions.decision: Verified the `autoSize: true` / internal `ResizeObserver` assumption in practice via an ad hoc Playwright script driven against the live dev server (not committed to the repo -- run and deleted during implementation), for all four chart panes, in addition to an added permanent Playwright e2e spec (`frontend/tests/e2e/stock-analysis.spec.ts`, the price-chart case) and the mocked vitest/Testing Library suite.
decisions.rationale: The task explicitly called for verifying this assumption in practice rather than trusting it from the option's name, and the mocked-`lightweight-charts` unit test suite can't exercise this at all (the mock has no `<canvas>`/`ResizeObserver` concept). The ad hoc script drag-resized and maximized each of the four panes against the actual running app and confirmed the real `<canvas>` element's own height grew along with its container in every case, with no `chart.resize()`/`applyOptions({width,height})` call anywhere in this app's code -- this is also what caught the Dialog-remount bug recorded in the sibling `decisions` entry above. The added e2e spec (one new `test(...)` case) gives this a permanent, repeatable check beyond this one-off manual pass; it wasn't runnable end-to-end through `yarn test:e2e`'s own Playwright-managed webServer during this session because a separate, already-running dev-server pair occupied the suite's hardcoded ports 8000/5173 (a standing constraint for this task: that dev server was not to be touched), so the new spec's correctness was instead confirmed by matching its selectors/assertions 1:1 against the ad hoc script that *was* run successfully against that live server.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #373 review's first blocking finding (no focus trap in the maximized overlay) with a hand-rolled focus trap directly in `ChartFrame.tsx`'s existing maximize `useEffect`, rather than pulling in a dependency (e.g. `focus-trap-react`, `@mui/base`'s standalone `FocusTrap`). It listens for `keydown` on `window` while maximized and, on `Tab`/`Shift+Tab`, computes the overlay's own focusable descendants (`getFocusableElements`, scoped to that instance's own `frameRef` subtree) and redirects focus back inside whenever it would otherwise land outside that subtree -- including wrapping at the first/last element and the edge case of focus still sitting on the dialog container itself (right after the existing initial `frameRef.current?.focus()`). It also now captures `document.activeElement` before stealing focus and restores it on close (the maximize-toggle button that triggered it), which the pre-fix version never did.
decisions.rationale: `package.json` has no existing focus-trap dependency and MUI's own `Dialog`/`Modal` -- the natural candidate, since this codebase already depends on `@mui/material` -- was already ruled out for this component by an earlier `decisions` entry (it unmounts/remounts the chart's container div and kills the Lightweight Charts canvas); pulling in `@mui/base`'s standalone, unstyled `FocusTrap` just to wrap the existing always-mounted `Box` was considered but rejected as needless indirection for a genuinely small, well-understood piece of logic (collect focusables, clamp Tab at the boundaries) that this component already had almost every piece of (the `keydown` listener, the `frameRef`, the initial-focus call) -- adding a new dependency (even one already transitively present via `@mui/material`) for ~30 lines of logic this component could implement directly, consistent with how it already reimplemented scroll-lock/Escape-handling instead of depending on `Dialog` for free, didn't pay for itself. Scoping `getFocusableElements` to the single instance's own `frameRef.current` (rather than, say, filtering by computed visibility) is what actually fixes the reported bug: the other, non-maximized pane's maximize button genuinely IS `display:flex`/`visibility:visible` (just z-index-stacked behind the overlay), so a visibility-based filter would not have told the two cases apart -- only DOM-subtree scoping does. Verified against a real, running dev server (not just the mocked vitest suite, since this is exactly the class of bug the task's own prior round's Dialog-remount bug was also only caught by a real browser, not jsdom): maximized the Price chart pane and pressed Tab 20 times and Shift+Tab 20 times via a throwaway Playwright script (not committed) against `/stocks/AAPL` on a freshly-started `make backend`/`make frontend` pair -- focus never left the dialog's own subtree in either direction, and Escape correctly restored focus to the 'View Price chart full screen' button that opened it.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #373 review's second blocking finding (per-instance body-scroll-lock snapshot/restore, fragile across two simultaneously-maximized instances) by replacing the per-instance `previousBodyOverflow` snapshot with a module-level open-overlay counter/stack (`openOverlayCount`/`bodyOverflowBeforeFirstOverlay`, `acquireBodyScrollLock()` in `ChartFrame.tsx`) -- only the FIRST `acquire` across all `ChartFrame` instances actually sets `document.body.style.overflow = 'hidden'` and snapshots the prior value, and only the release that brings the shared count back to 0 restores it.
decisions.rationale: This mirrors MUI's own `ModalManager` stacking approach, explicitly named in the review finding this fixes, and is the standard, well-understood pattern for this exact class of bug (multiple independent components competing to lock/unlock one shared, global piece of mutable state) -- a per-instance timestamp/generation-counter scheme or a React Context-based provider were both considered and rejected as more machinery than the problem needs: a module-level counter requires no additional provider wrapping every page that might render a `ChartFrame` (this component is meant to be usable standalone, per its own `common/` placement), and module-level state is safe here specifically because there's exactly one JS module instance of `ChartFrame.tsx` for the whole app (no micro-frontend/multiple-bundle concern in this codebase). Verified in the same real-browser Playwright walkthrough as the focus-trap fix above: maximized the Price chart pane (`overflow` -> `'hidden'`), then force-activated the Oscillators pane's own maximize button via a direct DOM `.focus()`+`.click()` (since the now-fixed focus trap makes this specific two-instances-open scenario unreachable through Tab alone, this reproduces it the same way the original bug report's own reproduction needed the focus-trap gap to reach it) -- both panes maximized simultaneously (2 dialogs), `overflow` stayed `'hidden'`. Closing the FIRST-opened instance (Price chart) while the second (Oscillators) was still maximized -- the exact out-of-open-order sequence the review described -- left `overflow` as `'hidden'` (the bug this fixes: the old per-instance snapshot would have restored it to `''` here, re-enabling page scroll while a dialog was still covering the viewport); only closing the last remaining maximized instance restored it to `''`.

decisions.decision: Folded in the easiest non-blocking follow-up from `frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json` during this needs_work round: gave the drag-to-resize handle (`role="separator"`) a keyboard equivalent -- `tabIndex={0}`, `aria-valuenow`/`aria-valuemin`/`aria-valuemax`, and an `onKeyDown` handler supporting ArrowUp/ArrowDown (20px steps, 100px with Shift) and Home/End (jump to the clamped min/max). Left the other three non-blocking findings on that followups task deferred, as the dispatch explicitly allowed.
decisions.rationale: This was the single cheapest of the four non-blocking findings to close (a focused, self-contained addition to the one component already being touched for the two blocking fixes, following the WAI-ARIA separator/window-splitter pattern's own recommended keyboard affordance), versus the other three (per-component maximize tests for the three non-PriceChart panes, a narrower per-pane `MAXIMIZED_CHROME_ALLOWANCE_PX`, and gating the window-resize subscription on `isMaximized`) which are each either more speculative in scope or lower-value relative to the risk of touching more of this already-changed file in the same pass. The followups task's checklist item for this is marked done there; its other three items remain open and untouched.

comments.summary: BLOCKING: the full-screen overlay declares `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"` but implements no focus trap, so keyboard focus can Tab straight out of the maximized overlay into the underlying page content that sits behind it (visually hidden by the opaque, fixed, full-viewport Box, but still present in the DOM and still focusable). Reproduced in a real browser: maximizing the Price chart pane and pressing Tab 11 times moves focus to the Oscillators pane's own 'View Oscillators full screen' button, which is not inside the dialog and is not visible on screen (confirmed via screenshot: the button's computed style is visibility:visible/display:flex but it sits entirely underneath the opaque overlay). A keyboard user can press Enter on that invisible, focused control without any visual indication of what will happen. The decisions entry for the Dialog-removal fix explicitly lists 'scroll-lock/Escape-handling/focus-placement' as the three Dialog behaviors reimplemented, but a focus trap (keeping Tab cycling confined to the open dialog) isn't one of them and isn't present anywhere in ChartFrame.tsx.

BLOCKING (confirmed by an independent code-review pass, not just this reviewer): the body-scroll-lock restore (`previousBodyOverflow`) is a per-instance snapshot with no shared open-count/stack, so two simultaneously-maximized ChartFrame instances closed out of open-order leave `document.body.style.overflow` wrong. Reachable via the focus-trap gap above: maximize chart A (captures `previous=''`, sets `overflow='hidden'`), Tab out through the focus-trap gap to chart B's own (hidden-behind-A) maximize button and activate it via keyboard (captures `previous='hidden'`, already 'hidden'), then close A first -- its cleanup restores `overflow` to its own captured `''`, re-enabling page scroll while B is still rendered as a full-viewport overlay. The same class of bug MUI's own Modal/ModalManager stack-count exists to prevent; fixing the focus trap alone doesn't remove this latent fragility in a shared `common/` component that could later be reused somewhere multiple instances are legitimately open at once.

Non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): the drag-to-resize handle (role="separator") has no keyboard equivalent at all -- not even focusable via Tab, let alone operable with arrow keys. The full-screen toggle gives keyboard users an alternative way to see a chart bigger, so this doesn't block, but it's a real WCAG 2.1.1 gap in the resize affordance itself. Independently flagged by both this review and a separate code-review pass.

Non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): no per-component test (vitest/Testing Library) exercises the maximize/resize wiring specifically for OscillatorChart, VolumeIndicatorsChart, or TrendStrengthChart -- only ChartFrame's own generic unit tests and one e2e spec scoped to PriceChart cover this in practice; the other three panes' wiring was verified only by this review's manual browser walkthrough.

Non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): MAXIMIZED_CHROME_ALLOWANCE_PX=220 is one constant shared across all four panes despite PriceChart's own chrome (range/interval controls + several legend rows) being visibly taller than the other three panes' single title row; the overflow:auto fallback covers this today (confirmed fine at a 900px viewport) but wasn't checked at a shorter (~700px) viewport height.

Non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): the window-resize `useSyncExternalStore` subscription (`subscribeToWindowResize`/`computeMaximizedHeight`) stays active for the component's whole lifetime regardless of `isMaximized`, so every browser resize/orientation-change re-renders all four chart panes even when none is maximized and the recomputed value is immediately discarded by `canvasHeight`'s non-maximized branch -- flagged by the separate code-review pass as a minor, avoidable render-churn cost (e.g. gate the subscription on `isMaximized`, or only recompute lazily on the read that actually needs it).

ROUND 2 (re-review): both blocking findings above are genuinely fixed, independently re-verified in a real browser against the exact originally-reported reproductions. Focus trap: maximized the Price chart pane and pressed Tab 20 times, then Shift+Tab 20 times -- focus never once left the dialog's own subtree in either direction (zero escapes), initial focus moved into the dialog on open, and focus correctly restored to the triggering 'View Price chart full screen' button on close (Escape). Scroll-lock stacking: maximized Price chart (`overflow` -> 'hidden'), force-activated Oscillators' own maximize button via a direct DOM `.focus()`+`.click()` (the same bypass the fix's own decisions entry used, since the now-fixed trap makes this unreachable via Tab alone) -- both panes maximized simultaneously, `overflow` stayed 'hidden'; closing the FIRST-opened instance (Price chart) while the second (Oscillators) was still maximized left `overflow` as 'hidden' (the exact bug this fixes -- the old per-instance snapshot would have restored it to '' here); only closing the last remaining instance restored it to ''. Keyboard-resize follow-up also verified working end to end: ArrowDown/ArrowUp step by 20px, Shift+Arrow by 100px, Home/End jump to the exact clamped [200, 900] bounds, and further Arrow presses past either bound stay clamped.

ROUND 2, non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): the new Tab-trap scopes 'inside the dialog' purely to `frameRef`'s own DOM subtree, which doesn't recognize a portaled MUI component (Popover/Menu/Autocomplete) opened from content inside the maximized overlay -- e.g. a MetricHelp/InfoBalloon '?' popover. Verified in a real browser and via a jsdom reproduction: opening such a popover while maximized and pressing Tab doesn't escape focus anywhere (MUI's own Modal/enforceFocus wins the resulting tug-of-war, keeping focus on the popover's own Paper every time; Escape still correctly closes just the popover first, then the dialog on a second press) -- no observable defect against this app's actual current content, since every MetricHelp/InfoBalloon/AnchoredInfoBalloon instance inside these four panes renders plain text with zero interactive elements (confirmed by grep). Would become a real keyboard-reachability bug the moment such a popover's content ever gained an interactive element.

ROUND 2, non-blocking (tracked as docs/tasks/frontend-chart-fullscreen-resize-followups.json): the focus trap is per-instance only, with no cross-instance coordination (unlike the sibling scroll-lock fix's shared counter) -- if two instances were ever simultaneously maximized, each instance's own window-level Tab listener would fight to redirect focus back into itself, with the later-registered (topmost) instance winning only by registration-order coincidence, not design. Confirmed unreachable today via an ordinary mouse click (a real, actionability-checked Playwright click on a background pane's maximize button times out -- the foreground overlay's `position: fixed` genuinely intercepts the pointer event at the browser's hit-testing level) and via keyboard (the now-fixed trap prevents Tabbing to it). Related: `ChartFrame` doesn't apply `aria-hidden`/`inert` to background content while maximized (unlike MUI's own Modal/ModalManager), so this state might be reachable by a screen-reader user in virtual-cursor/browse mode bypassing both the visual occlusion and the Tab interception -- plausible but not independently verified against a real screen reader in this review (none available in this environment).
